content: Specificity was evaluated in healthy individuals who had negative results on interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs). The difference in specificity was calculated as the variation in the proportion of negative results between Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) and either the tuberculin skin test (TST) or IGRAs in healthy populations. Across five studies, the specificity of all three TBSTs was high, as shown in Figure 5. However, the overall certainty of the evidence regarding the specificity of these tests was rated as very low due to the inclusion of studies of very low quality. In children and adolescents (two studies, 176 participants), specificity was also high when assessed in individuals with negative IGRA results. The pooled difference in specificity across 14 studies showed that TBSTs had a higher specificity (8%) compared to TSTs, with variations potentially explained by differences in Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination rates or test cut-offs used in the studies. The risk of bias in these studies was considered serious because test allocation was not blinded in most cases, except for studies involving Cy-Tb. Additionally, the selection of participants and the reference standard diagnosis were unclear in many Diaskintest studies. As a result, the certainty of evidence for the difference in specificity between TBSTs and TSTs was downgraded to low due to both risk of bias and inconsistency in findings. Agreement between TBSTs and comparator tests (TST or IGRAs) was assessed in 16 studies involving 3,198 participants, including four studies with 1,307 participants under 18 years of age. In individuals without tuberculosis (TB) disease, agreement was high (≥90%) for Cy-Tb and Diaskintest when compared to QuantiFERON (QFT). However, the certainty of evidence for agreement between TBSTs and IGRAs was rated as low due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency in findings, with agreement ranging from 61% to 97% across studies. A systematic review of safety outcomes, including local injection site reactions (ISRs) and systemic adverse events, identified seven studies for Cy-Tb, five for C-TST, and 11 for Diaskintest. Most Cy-Tb studies were conducted in South Africa and Europe, with a significant proportion of participants living with HIV in South African studies. The pooled risk of any ISR due to Cy-Tb was assessed as high-certainty evidence, while evidence for systemic reactions was judged as moderate-certainty due to small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals. Diaskintest studies reported 27 serious adverse events and 30 non-serious adverse events out of 1.7 million tests performed, with the overall safety profile deemed similar to that of TST. Cost and cost-effectiveness analyses were conducted using systematic reviews and a Markov-chain model. The reviews assessed the economic evaluations of novel TBSTs (e.g., Diaskintest, C-TST, Cy-Tb) and existing tests (TST and IGRAs). The quality of studies assessing the cost-effectiveness of TBSTs was concerning, with only one out of eight studies rated as high quality. In Brazil and South Africa, Diaskintest was found to be cost-saving compared to TST and IGRAs, while in the United Kingdom, it was cost-saving compared to TST but not IGRAs. User perspectives on the value, feasibility, usability, and acceptability of diagnostic technologies were explored through systematic reviews, interviews, and a discrete choice experiment (DCE). Key end-user values included test accuracy, convenience, positive patient experience, and cost. Users preferred tests that minimized false positives and negatives, were easy to administer, and did not require follow-up visits. TBSTs were perceived as having greater specificity and sensitivity than TSTs, but IGRAs were preferred in settings where the necessary infrastructure was already in place. Implementation considerations for TBSTs include the need for regulatory approval, appropriate communication about the new tests, cold chain requirements, skilled staff for administration and interpretation, and effective stock management. TBSTs are likely to be more feasible in settings where TST is already in use, but IGRAs may be more practical in settings with existing infrastructure to support them.
